I don't have much to disagree with you on, but I will take up the conversation about the second amendment once more. As a preface: I live in Illinois, have a FOID card, own an AR-15, and many other guns. I like guns. My gun safe is full of neat toys and valuable tools.

Read Stevens's dissent in Heller, though. The preamble to the second amendment wasn't included for fun, it conveyed meaning about the intent of the amendment. Additionally, there is historical evidence that language was recommended from some states and considered when the bill of rights was written that would have made an unalienable, individual right to own and possess arms explicit. That that language was rejected seems to clearly indicate that the second amendment was not written with the intent to put restrictions on the power of our legislatures to put limits on who can own which arms and where.

Historically, this was the position of the Court (see US v Miller for one example). It is only in the last few decades that public opinion on this began to change, and for obvious reasons in my opinion. The majority opinion in Heller was, astonishingly (given the originalist bent of that court), completely out of line with historical jurisprudence and historical evidence for the original intent. The logic used in the majority opinion was tortured, to be kind. Then retired Chief Justice Warren Burger said in 1990:

The Gun Lobby's interpretation of the Second Amendment is one of the greatest pieces of fraud, I repeat the word fraud, on the American people by special interest groups that I have ever seen in my lifetime. The real purpose of the Second Amendment was to ensure that state armies - the militia - would be maintained for the defense of the state. The very language of the Second Amendment refutes any argument that it was intended to guarantee every citizen an unfettered right to any kind of weapon he or she desires.

No new evidence was considered during Heller. It was pure judicial activism. Again, I like guns. I like that I can own guns. But, either my preferences don't matter, or intellectual honesty doesn't matter.

Based on the prior case law, the dissent had the better opinion, no doubt. The majority used no federal case law. Scalia tried to analogize state constitutional provisions that were obviously differently worded as if they said the same thing. Scalia's mocking of the Stevens dissent's analysis of the "keep and bare arms" term was laughable. Of course the "prefatory clause" had meaning and Stevens destroyed Scalia on that issue. Stevens for his own part did some serious stretching, but at least he had federal case law on his side.

As I said, I agree with the Heller result. I would have decided differently notwithstanding the earlier precedent. I would have said more simply that the people are the militia (this was the major outstanding issue), that hand guns are the preferred weapon of citizens, and that an entire city cannot essentially ban ownership of operating hand guns under the Second Amendment.

As for the later McDonald case, I don't even get why that was an issue. It seemed plain obvious to me that the Constitution would apply outside DC. This is the stuff of conspiracies. But I got major laughs watching the "conservatives" rushing to defend the 14th Amendment which they would like to oppose. They did a very good job too! Now, if they would apply it across the board instead of merely when they want a desired outcome .... :)

Countdown to Extinction is one of the best albums of the 90s. I don't care what anybody says, I think it is far better than Metallica's work from that era. Everything about the album is just spot-on--from the guitar work to the production and vocals--it remains one of the most perfectly executed hard-rock albums of all time.

It is a superb album in it's own right, but looking at it as a follow up to Rust in Peace makes it feel like a let down. Then again Rust in Peace is absolute thrash perfection so I couldn't see how Dave could possibly top that album.

Rust in Peace is awesome as well--one of my all-time favorites. But like you said, it is a thrash-metal album and as such had more limited appeal. Countdown to Extinction retained (and expanded) much of what made Rust great, but added just enough traditional hard-rock elements to make the album understandable to a broader audience. To put a finer point on it, I'd recommend Countdown to almost anyone who likes hard-rock. Rust--at least for me--sort of requires a listener to already have an affinity for no-bullshit thrash. That might not be the case any longer as both albums are ~25 years old, and maybe fresh, young ears don't discriminate like they used to...but back in the day, Rust was just raw enough that it's appeal was limited to fans of the genre, whereas Countdown broke through to the mainstream in a big way. Either way, both albums are fucking awesome...and thinking about it just now, I favor Rust myself. Megadeth remains one of my all-time favorite bands, and I don't even like metal that much.
